summary: A first attempt at giving Internet users and site administrators guidance on handling security issues. It is an FYI informational document and was replaced by RFC 2196.

eli5.summary: It is a safety guide for people who run computers, telling them how to keep them safe. A newer guide has replaced it.

subtitle: How to create security policies and procedures for networked computer sites.

tldr.problem: Computer sites connected to the Internet face security threats from intruders and misconfigured systems, but few had written policies or procedures for dealing with them.
tldr.mechanism: This handbook walks site administrators through creating security policies (what to protect and why), preventive procedures (passwords, monitoring, access control), and incident handling plans (how to respond when breaches occur).
tldr.outcome: Organizations can establish systematic security policies, train staff, and respond to incidents more effectively. RFC 2196 replaced this with a more comprehensive version.

facts.label: Key problem
facts.value: 80% or more of security issues involved poorly chosen passwords

today: RFC 2196 superseded this handbook with a revised and expanded version covering more modern threats and environments.

sections.title: Why Security Policies and Procedures Matter
sections.content:
In the early 1990s, computers were becoming networked and distributed; they were no longer locked in secure data centers. The Internet connected systems worldwide, but also exposed them to attacks from outside the organization. Traditional security (locked doors and physical guards) no longer sufficed. Site administrators and decision makers needed to understand the risks and threats their systems faced, and decide what actions to take.

This handbook is the first attempt to provide systematic guidance to Internet site administrators on setting security policies and procedures. It addresses what a site must protect, how to prevent problems, and what to do when breaches occur. The guide is necessarily incomplete and focuses mostly on U.S. resources; different organizations and jurisdictions may have different needs and regulations.
sections.eli5: Computers used to be in locked rooms with guards. Now they are connected to the world on the Internet, so managers need written plans for keeping them safe.

sections.title: Creating an Official Security Policy
sections.content:
A security policy is a written document that defines what the organization needs to protect and why. Effective policy creation requires agreement from both technical staff (who understand what is feasible) and decision makers (who have authority to enforce it). A key element is risk assessment: identifying assets, threats, and the likelihood of harm, then spending money in a cost-effective way to address the greatest risks.

The policy should cover what happens when the policy is violated, who is responsible for different aspects of security, and how to interpret the policy in ambiguous situations. Once written, the policy must be publicized through meetings and training, not just mailed out. Users and administrators should sign a statement confirming they have read and understood the policy, which may be important for legal action if violations occur.
sections.eli5: A written plan says what computers and information the organization cares about, who might try to steal or break them, and what the organization will do about it. Everyone needs to know and agree to the plan.

sections.title: Preventive Procedures and Security Controls
sections.content:
Once policies are in place, procedures spell out exactly how to protect assets. Common areas include account management (removing default vendor accounts, enforcing password changes), configuration management (checking system installations for insecure defaults), system monitoring (checking logs regularly for suspicious activity), and physical security (locking up critical servers). The document emphasizes that password management is critical: 80% of security problems involved weak passwords.

Other procedures include regular backups, use of encryption for sensitive data, authentication systems like Kerberos, network firewalls to limit outside access, and monitoring tools to detect unauthorized use. The key is to use multiple strategies: if one protection is bypassed, another still protects the asset. Common sense is more important than elaborate mechanisms; a single user with a weak password can undermine any complex security scheme.
sections.eli5: Day-to-day steps like changing passwords, checking who is logged in, backing up files, and locking doors. Many simple protections together are stronger than one fancy lock.

sections.title: Incident Handling and Response
sections.content:
A security incident is when someone breaches the policy (an intruder attack, a virus, an insider misusing an account). Effective incident handling requires a written plan and preparation. The goal is to respond in a planned, systematic way rather than in panic when an attack occurs. The handbook outlines five key steps: evaluation (is it really an incident?), notification (who to call and how), response (what actions to take), legal considerations (whether to call law enforcement, how to preserve evidence), and documentation (keeping records for later analysis).

Priorities matter during an incident: protect human life first, then sensitive data, then other data, then systems, then minimize disruption. The site should prepare a contact list in advance with phone numbers and roles (technical staff, management, legal, law enforcement). During an incident, communicate factually and clearly without alarming language or speculation. After the incident, capture lessons learned and improve policies based on what happened.
sections.eli5: When something bad happens, a site needs a plan for who to call, how to stop the damage, and how to tell if it really is an attack. After, learn what went wrong and fix it.

sections.title: Resources and Response Teams
sections.content:
Several support resources exist to help sites handle security. The CERT/CC (Computer Emergency Response Team, established by DARPA in 1988) is operated by Carnegie Mellon University and provides a 24-hour hotline for sites to report security problems. The CERT identifies and coordinates fixes for vulnerabilities, and distributes security advisories. The DDN Security Coordination Center serves similar functions for Defense Data Network users. Specialized teams like NIST's Computer Security Resource and Response Center and DOE's Computer Incident Advisory Capability (CIAC) also assist sites.

Mailing lists and USENET newsgroups (UNIX Security, comp.security.announce, VIRUS-L) provide advance notice of problems. The handbook includes an annotated bibliography covering computer law, ethics, security checklists, and cryptography. Sites should establish relationships with external response teams and law enforcement before an incident occurs, so they know who to contact and what evidence is needed for prosecution.
sections.eli5: There are organizations (like CERT) with experts who help sites with security problems. Subscribe to their mailing lists to hear about new threats before they hurt your systems.
